Madanapārijāta
------------------------------------------
The Madanapārijāta is an extensive digest of dharmaśāstra by Viśveśvara भट्ट, written probably during the period A. D. 1360-1390. He was a court pundit of the king Madanapāla who was the ruler of a small state north of Delhi, on the bank of the river यमुना.
His other work is the Subodhinī, a commentary on the Mitākṣarā of विज्ञानेश्वर (12th century A. D.). (See VIJÑĀNEŚVARA.)
The contents of the Madanapārijāta may briefly be stated as follows: ब्रह्मचर्य (studenthood), duties of householders, the various सṁस्कारस् or sacraments, śrāddha (obsequial rites), अशौच (ceremonial impurity), दायभाग (See DĀYABHĀGA for details.) and prāyaś-cittas (expiations).

Madālasā
------------------------------------------
Madālasā is one of the great women described in the पुराणस् (vide Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa 20-44) who was a devoted wife as also a worthy मोथेर्.
She was the exquisitely beautiful daughter of the gandharva king Viśvāvasu. A demon, Pātālaketu by name, once abducted her but was rescued by the prince Ṛtadhvaja (also known as Kuvalayāśva) who married her later. She remained extremely devoted and faithful to him.
Once when she was falsely informed that her husband had died, she gave up her body immediately in extreme grief. She was however revived by Aśvatara, a नाग king, whose sons were Ṛtadhvaja’s friends.
She is said to have been a great yoginī and imparted आत्मज्ञान or Self-knowledge to her first three sons who became recluses. The fourth, Alarka succeeded the king Ṛtadhvaja.

Madanaratna
------------------------------------------
The Madanaratna—also known as Madanaratnapradīpa and Madanapradīpa—is a voluminous compendium of धर्म-śāstra. It is attributed to Viśvanātha, son of Bhaṭṭapūjya and a resident of काशी. He was a court pundit under the king Madanasiṁha and probably lived during the period A. D. 1400-1450.
The work is in seven sections called ‘uddyotas’ (‘that which sheds light’). They are: samaya (time), आचार (conduct), vyavahāra (legal procedures), प्रायश्चित्त (expiations), दान (gifts), शुद्धि (purificatory rites) and śānti (propitiatory rites).
Only a few sections have been published.

mada
(‘intoxication’, ‘arrogance’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptures describe six evil qualities of the मिन्द् which are enemies in the path of moral and spiritual evolution and hence called ‘ariṣaḍvarga’ (ari = enemy, ṣaṭ = six). मद is one of them and is generally placed as the fifth in the series.
Mada is intoxication born out of several factors. At the psychological level it is translated as arrogance.
Some of the factors which produce this मद or arrogance are: विद्या (learning), dhana (wealth), कुल (lineage), yauvana (youth), बल (physical strength), rūpa (beauty), rājya (kingdom), parivāra (large retinue) and अधिकार (power).
Even तपस् (austerities) and सिद्धिस् (psychic powers) can cause मद if one is not careful and vigilant.

Madurai
(‘that [which is sweet like] honey’)
------------------------------------------
One of the famous places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in South India, Madurai—also spelt as Madhurai or Madhurā—is 461 kms. (286 miles) to the south-west of Chennai (Madras) and is situated on the bank of the Vaigai river. It is famous for its majestic temples, especially those of Mīnākṣī (an aspect of the Divine मोथेर् पार्वती) and Sundareśvara (Śiva).
Mīnākṣī TempleThe city itself is very ancient and the rulers of the Pāṇḍya dynasty who are mentioned even in the edicts of अशोक (circa 272-232 B. C.), had business contacts with the Roman empire. It was also an ancient seat of Tamil learning with 48 poets adorning the Saṅgam or college hall. However, the modern मदुरै attained the present state of progress and civilisation under the Nāyak kings.
According to the स्थलपुराण (local lores) इन्द्र, the king of the gods, after his defeat at the hands of वृत्रासुर, was roaming about as a human being in a forest. At a particular spot he felt great peace and happiness. There, he found a शिवलिङ्ग and worshipped Lord शिव through it. He immediately had a vision of शिव and got back his royal throne through शिव’s grace. It is at this spot that the local king built his capital city and named it मधुरा as per the wonderful dream he had, in which he saw अमृत or nectar being poured over the place (madhu = sweet; honey; nectar).
Regarding the goddess Mīnākṣī there is another interesting story. She was पार्वती reborn as the daughter of the Pāṇḍyan king Malayadhvaja. Since her eyes resembled a mīna (fish) she was given the name ‘Mīnākṣī’ (one whose eyes resemble a fish). She succeeded him as the ruler of the kingdom, routed all the enemies and established her supremacy. She fell in love with Sundareśvara (Śiva, born as a human being) and was married to him. विष्णु himself acted as the brother of Mīnākṣī in this मर्रिअगे. He is known as ‘Aḷahar’. His temple is at the foot of a hillock, at a distance of 21 kms. (13 miles) from मदुरै.
The most important of the several temples is the Mīnākṣī temple complex situated on a site 258 metres (850 ft.) by 241 metres (700 ft.). There are two main shrines, dedicated to Mīnākṣī and Sunda-reśvara (Śiva), no less than twelve gopurams (towers), a tank and a large number of maṇḍapas or halls. The actual dimensions of the twin shrines along with the various halls and associated structures is 68.5 metres (225 ft.) by 45.7 metres (150 ft.)
The sanctum sanctorum of the goddess Mīnākṣī is a square of 10.4 metres (34 ft.). Elephants, lions and dwarfs are shown as supporting the structure. On the outer walls, there are prominent niches projecting to a length of 1.8 metres (3 1/4 ft.) and containing many images like the Liṅgodbhavamūrti (Śiva emerging out of the लिङ्ग), दक्षिणामूर्ति (an aspect of शिव) and दुर्गा. The विमान (small tower) above the sanctum has three storeys.
The lovely Golden Lily tank, the Citragopura with 740 sculptures, the Āyirakkāl or thousand-pillared मण्डप, murals and paintings including a museum, the musical pillars (of stone) and a six-pillared ध्वज-stambha or flagstaff are the other attractions.
The Tirumala Nāyak palace (called the Mahal), temple of Aḷagar or Aḷahar, the Māriamman Teppakulam (tank)—these are the other attractions.
The main festivals are: the मर्रिअगे of the goddess with Sundareśvara during April/May, चोरोनतिओन् of Lord Sunda-reśvara during August/September, and the teppotsava or float-festival in January/ February.
See also MĪNĀKṢĪ.
